extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in 19th-century clipper ships and maritime history
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and documents the standards, rules, performance metrics, and practices used aboard mid‑19th century emigrant clippers (navigation, ship construction, passenger regulations, entertainment, provisioning, and discipline). Useful for understanding how such ships were evaluated and operated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 1: No smoking or naked light allowed below
rubrics_metrics.description: 1st. No smoking or naked light allowed below.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Posted prominently aboard the ship as a fire-safety rule. No additional guidance given on enforcement beyond the general penalties for noncompliance (see Rule 15).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 2: Lights out by 10 p.m. (except hatchway lights)
rubrics_metrics.description: 2nd. All lights, except the hatchway lights, to be put out by 10 p.m.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A curfew-based lighting rule to reduce fire risk and preserve order at night.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 3: No Congreve matches in berths or lower deck
rubrics_metrics.description: 3rd. No Congreve matches to be used in the berths or on the lower deck.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific prohibition on a dangerous ignition source; part of the shipboard fire-safety regimen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 4: Cleanliness and decorum strictly observed
rubrics_metrics.description: 4th. Cleanliness and decorum to be strictly observed at all times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broad behavioral and hygiene expectation enforced shipwide; linked elsewhere to daily inspections and surgeon oversight (see Rule 5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 5: Daily cleaning below for surgeon and chief officer inspection
rubrics_metrics.description: 5th. Every place below to be well cleaned every day after breakfast, for the inspection of the surgeon and chief officer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies timing (after breakfast) and inspectors (surgeon and chief officer). Connects cleanliness to health oversight and discipline aboard emigrant ships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 6: Bedding to be aired on deck twice weekly
rubrics_metrics.description: 6th. All bedding to be on deck twice a week.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hygiene procedure (airing/sunning bedding) to reduce infestation/illness; typical practice on long voyages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 7: ’Tween deck passengers appoint constables to preserve order
rubrics_metrics.description: 7th. The ’tween deck passengers to appoint constables to preserve order and see these rules are strictly observed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delegation of internal discipline to passenger-elected constables as part of self-policing among steerage passengers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 8: Duties and rewards for passenger constables
rubrics_metrics.description: 8th. The constables are to keep watch in their respective compartments for their own safety and that of their families; trim the lamps; report all misdemeanours, for which they will receive a glass of grog or a cup of coffee every morning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies constable duties (watch, lamp maintenance, reporting) and incentive (daily grog/coffee).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 9: Second cabin promenade restriction (windward side prohibited)
rubrics_metrics.description: 9th. Second cabin passengers are not allowed on the windward side of the vessel; but can promenade at all hours on the leeward side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforces class-based spatial segregation for safety/comfort; specifies permitted promenade area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 10: ’Tween deck ports closed without express permission
rubrics_metrics.description: 10th. Passengers must not upon any account open the ’tween deck ports without my express permission: a violation of this rule may be attended with serious consequences, and will, in any case, be severely punished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Safety rule forbidding opening of ventilation/sea-ports without permission; warns of serious consequences and severe punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 11: Dancing and promenading times/locations on the poop
rubrics_metrics.description: 11th. Dancing and promenading on the poop from 7 till 9 p.m., when all passengers may enjoy themselves, but not abaft the mizen mast. The promenaders are not in any way to interrupt the dancers, but will be expected to promenade in parts of the poop where dancing is not being carried on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schedules and spatial rules for social activities to avoid conflicts between different passenger groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 12: Third-class access to quarterdeck limited to 7–9 p.m.
rubrics_metrics.description: 12th. On account of the overcrowded state of the poop and to satisfy all parties, third class passengers are only allowed on the quarterdeck from 7 till 9 in the evening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time-limited access to upper deck spaces for steerage/third-class passengers to manage crowding and class relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 13: Private saloon staircase prohibited after 11 p.m.
rubrics_metrics.description: 13th. The use of the private staircase (into the saloon) is strictly prohibited after 11 at night.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restricts access between passenger classes/areas during late hours for security and decorum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 14: No speaking to officers or quartermasters while on duty
rubrics_metrics.description: 14th. No person allowed to speak to the officers of the watch whilst on duty: nor to any of the quartermasters, whilst at the wheel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protects the watch and wheel from interruption for safety and operational discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 15: Punishment by deduction of provisions for noncompliance
rubrics_metrics.description: 15th. All parties not complying with these rules will be liable to have a part of their provisions deducted as a punishment, as the commander and officers may think fit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies an explicit, non-physical penalty (reduction of provisions) enforceable by commander/officers for rule violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ship performance: passage duration and 24-hour run as evaluation metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Voyage performance is reported and evaluated by total days out (passage duration) and by daily runs (miles in 24 hours) — e.g., runs of 421 miles in 24 hours, 368 miles best run, passages of 64–100+ days, averages (Donald Mackay average 83 days).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to compare ships, captains and voyages; the text cites exact examples and tables of 'best outward passages' and 'best homeward passages' to rank performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ship construction and measurements as quality indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Ships are described and compared by registered/gross/net tonnage, length (keel, overall, between perpendiculars), beam, depth, dead rise, sail area, mainyard length, and mast weight (e.g., Donald Mackay registered tonnage 2408, mainmast nearly 20 tons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dimensional and tonnage data indicate cargo capacity, seaworthiness and potential speed; numerous examples provided for multiple ships to allow comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sail plan and rigging innovations
rubrics_metrics.description: Notable rigging and sail-plan features are treated as evaluative/innovative: e.g., Forbes’ patent double topsail yards (topmasts fidded abaft lower masts), crossing three skysail yards, absence of moonsail, heavy built masts banded with iron.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Innovations in sail plan are flagged as novelties and as differentiators among ships; such features affect performance and handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shipbuilding technique and materials as durability indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Construction methods and materials (e.g., three skins—two diagonal and one fore-and-aft—fastened with screw-threaded hardwood trunnels) are noted as novelties and affect strength and cost (Schomberg cost £43,103).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique (skinning, fastenings, heavy rigging) used to judge robustness and expense; included as causes for expectations of performance or failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Captain seamanship: risk-taking vs safety
rubrics_metrics.description: Captains are judged by navigational audacity and passage-making (e.g., Black Ball captains celebrated for daring navigation; McDonald nearly ashore three times) but also by prudence — examples where risk or negligence (Forbes on Schomberg) led to stranding and scandal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance between taking calculated risks to 'make a good passage' and the duty to avoid endangering ship and passengers; post‑voyage inquiries and passenger censures are part of evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Captain leadership, discipline and tact as indicators of a 'well-run' emigrant ship
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualities such as tact, impartiality, fairness, strict but just discipline, and ability to control a mixed passenger body are praised (Captain Enright described as a Puritan, stern disciplinarian but tactful), while lack of discipline is linked to bad food, riots, gambling and general disorder (Royal Charter example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leadership style is explicitly tied to passenger morale and shipboard order; the captain's character and treatment of crew/passengers are core evaluative criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passenger management and class segregation practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedures for managing mixed-class passenger communities are given: appointment of passenger constables, spatial/time restrictions for promenading and deck use by class, prohibition of certain accesses (private staircase), and separate entertainments (each class had its own concerts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational rules intended to preserve order, safety and class expectations on long emigrant voyages; examples include timetable windows for promenade (7–9 p.m.) and third-class quarterdeck access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shipboard entertainment and morale maintenance
rubrics_metrics.description: Keeping passengers amused was important: ship's bands for daily dancing, concerts (class and 'Grand Monster Concert'), dances like polka and quadrille, mock trials, debates, choral societies, St. Valentine’s Day events, and other organized amusements (parades, deck games).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entertainment measured by frequency and variety; captain-sponsored events (e.g., St. Valentine’s Day) and passenger productions (ship newspapers) served to dissipate boredom and reduce disorder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shipboard newspaper practice and editorial policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Many ships carried a printing press; ship newspapers were edited by passengers (editor/sub-editor elected), the printer usually a paid crewman, and the captain acted as censor: 'no matter of a controversial sort either religious, political or otherwise being ever allowed to appear in the news sheet of Captain Enright’s ship.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy constrained content to avoid controversy; newspapers were important for morale and community, but subject to captain's censorship as part of maintaining order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Health and hygiene oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: Health practices included daily cleaning inspections by the surgeon and chief officer, airing bedding twice weekly, exercise (swabbers at pump described as 'capital exercise, strongly recommended'), and a Health Office notice board for roles like washerwoman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surgeon involvement in hygiene and organized exercise were formalized; hygiene practices were enforced and inspected to reduce disease risk on long voyages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisioning and food quality as passenger welfare indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: First-cabin bill of fare demonstrates high-quality provisioning (varied soups, fish, meats, sweets, dessert fruits and wines like champagne). Provisions could also be used as punitive deduction (Rule 15).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quality and variety of food indicate standard of accommodation and affect passenger satisfaction; provisioning was also a lever for discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Onboard commercial and social economy (purser sales, auctions, raffles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ships maintained a notice board listing purser sales (clothing, cigarettes), raffles (e.g., model ship shares), auctions on the poop, 'For Sale' and 'Found' notices — forming an onboard economy and social life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These practices structured social interaction, provided diversion and commerce, and are part of how a voyage's success and passenger contentment were measured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of quantitative voyage records (tables) to compare ships and captains
rubrics_metrics.description: The text uses tabulated records (best outward/homeward passages listing ship, captain, dates, days out, gold carried) as a means to rank performance across ships and years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit tabulation of voyages is a standard evaluative method for comparing passage-making ability and commercial success of lines and captains.
